voiceover: The numbers that unsettled the physicists. In the late 1970s, the physicist Paul Davies began collecting a strange inventory: places where the universe balances on a knife's edge. Empty space carries an energy — and it has to be vanishingly small, or galaxies could never have formed. Theory and observation differ by about a hundred and twenty orders of magnitude. Roger Penrose — no theist — calculated the precision of the universe's starting state. The number is so vast you could not write out its zeros, even with one on every particle in the observable universe. Stars can only forge carbon because of one precise energy level in the carbon nucleus. Fred Hoyle predicted it in 1953, and it was found essentially where he said. These figures come from mainstream physics, not apologetics. Hoyle, an unbeliever for most of his life, later wrote that the facts suggest a superintellect has monkeyed with physics. The data are measured. Design is the inference — and a mind behind the dials explains them better than the alternatives. The heavens declare the glory of God.
